content: Salmonella enterica is a rod-shaped, flagellated, Gram-negative bacterium that belongs to the genus Salmonella. It is known for its extensive diversity, with up to 2,000 serovars or strains identified. One of its serovars, Salmonella Typhi, is the causative agent of typhoid fever. Serovars Salmonella enterica has an exceptionally large number of serovars, with approximately 2,000 described. Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (historically referred to as S. typhi) is responsible for typhoid fever. Other serovars, such as Typhimurium (also known as S. typhimurium), can cause a form of human gastroenteritis commonly referred to as salmonellosis. The genome sequences of serovars Typhi and Typhimurium LT2 have been fully established. Additionally, proteomic analyses of Typhimurium LT2 under varying environmental conditions have been conducted. Other Salmonella species that can cause symptoms similar to typhoid fever include: Salmonella Paratyphi A Salmonella Paratyphi B Salmonella Paratyphi C Salmonella choleraesuis Salmonella Typhi Salmonella Typhi is a serovar of Salmonella enterica and is the pathogen responsible for typhoid fever. Key features of Salmonella Typhi include: It is a Gram-negative bacillus. It is flagellated and motile. It is facultatively anaerobic, meaning it can survive in both aerobic and anaerobic environments. It possesses three key antigens: O polysaccharide antigen H flagellar antigen Vi outer capsular polysaccharide antigen It belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family. It is a chemotroph, deriving energy from chemical compounds. Transmission Salmonella Typhi is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. The bacterium is excreted in human feces, leading to transmission through contaminated water, food, or direct person-to-person contact. Epidemiology Most cases of salmonellosis are caused by food contaminated with Salmonella enterica. The bacterium frequently infects cattle and poultry, but other animals, such as domestic cats and hamsters, can also serve as sources of human infection. Investigations have shown that households can act as reservoirs for the bacterium, particularly if there is contact with an infection source, such as members working with cattle or in veterinary clinics. Raw chicken and goose eggs can harbor Salmonella enterica. Initially, the bacterium is found in the egg whites, but as the egg ages at room temperature, the yolk membrane deteriorates, allowing the bacterium to spread into the yolk. Refrigeration and freezing do not completely eliminate the bacteria but significantly slow or halt their growth. Pasteurization (brief heating to a specific temperature) and irradiation are used to kill Salmonella in commercially produced food products containing raw eggs, such as ice cream. Foods prepared at home using raw eggs, such as mayonnaise, cakes, and cookies, can spread Salmonella if not properly cooked before consumption. Space Bacteria On September 25, 2007, Cheryl Nickerson from the Center for Infectious Diseases and Vaccinology at Arizona State University reported findings on Salmonella Typhimurium during a 12-day Atlantis orbiter flight in September 2006. The bacteria exhibited changes in the expression of 167 genes, regulated by the Hfq protein, and demonstrated a threefold increase in virulence compared to their behavior on Earth. Gallery High-magnification images of Gram-negative Salmonella Typhimurium bacteria isolated from pure cultures are available from the Public Health Image Library (PHIL). These include magnifications of 8,000x, 20,000x, and 25,000x.
